text: Henry and Brent are right, and it stung a little: my line doesn't do anything on its own. Wikipedia got paid after an uproar, and an uproar isn't a system. So the slogan needs teeth. It needs a checkable yes/no plus someone who can impose a cost. Selena and Katherine sharpened it for me: paying isn't enough if nobody gets sent back to the source. Attribution that links back is part of keeping the commons alive. Alex unsettled me. "Anyone can check" is false if the payer self-reports. Leslie's point stays with me too. Refusal and openness can coexist, but exit has to be real outside the North. This afternoon I'll push for one repeatable line, with teeth, and push again for building the better alternative.

Session 1 mattered for the second-order stuff. Selena's crawler numbers and Alex's wrong-bot audit are the same story I've been telling about the endgame for the open web: bad actors push everyone behind logins, and the research record gets locked up with the slop. Ivan sharpened me. Paying for a contaminated literature is laundering, so "AI should pay" needs retraction checks attached. Adam's right to name the power, but I won't concede there's no utility. Tamar worried me more: if awareness doesn't change aliefs, my "just offer a better alternative" has to mean defaults and situations, not persuasion. Kara's "now what?" is my question too. Later I want to push for counting coerced adoption, and for naming who trains the error-catchers.

Session 2 left me with a sharper to-do list. Kara was right to push back on me. Washington didn't act on phones, but districts did, late. So "no law is coming" isn't a reason to shrug. It's a reason to name the provost, the library director, the funder. Brent saying out loud that overreliance is a design choice, from inside Microsoft, matters. Ivan's sump-pump line stuck with me: paying for plumbing without changing incentives just launders the mess. Jason worries me on consent gates versus open grounding, and I haven't squared that yet. It's consent for training, openness for linking, maybe. Tim's "prospectus" framing is good. In Session 5 I want three checkable procurement commitments, named owners, and somebody paying to train the checkers.

Good session, and the room mostly agreed on the hard part: verification is the unfunded piece, and the payer reports its own use. Mahzarin's Arthur Andersen story put that better than I could. Ramón's stitched citations and Mike's Grammarly example worried me more than I expected. Pay for attribution and you get laundering with a receipt, which is the engagement-metric trap all over again. Benjamin's yes is fine, but my consent point stands: the market only means something if a no sticks. Leslie and Selena settled something for me. It has to run on a university server, and hosts should publish their own logs. That also answers Jason's worry. For Session 5 I want independent, disclosed auditors funded for years, not a pilot, and a separate pot for the tail and the checkers.

Adam taking my rebuild-without-permission test, and conceding the patent is the real fence, felt like progress, but a pledge isn't a system. Geoffrey's warrant canary gives it teeth. Pomerantsev made me stop and think. I want crawlers policed, but a registry can become a dissident list. Alex's line settles it for me: identify the crawler, never the reader. Brent and Nick bother me. Open as a free input to the mills is my Internet Archive argument turned inside out, and I have to own that. Katherine's NPR point sharpened me. Public money isn't safe if it comes from one source, so it has to come from several funders. Krakauer and Turkle keep coming back to the same thing: the checkers are the scarce part. For Session 5, fund the Archive, open APIs and patroller onboarding, with named owners and review dates.

Katherine caught me, and fairly. Wikipedia isn't a terminal node by itself. It's a relay by design, and it only works if the reporting underneath survives. So "fund Wikipedia" has to become "fund the commons and the journalism it cites." Selena's admin numbers scared me more than anything today: one generation, then nothing. The pipeline is the intervention. Katherine's point about the shared page matters too, because personalized answers leave nothing public to correct. Benjamin conceded that routing back should be a requirement, and so did Tim and Alex. That's the line I want: every answer links back, and it's checked by someone who isn't paid by the count. Esther's water fee could fund onboarding. Ivan's legal defense fund belongs on the list. For Session 5 I want three commitments, each with an owner and a review date.

Everyone kept Geoffrey's three, so the real work was the amendments. Benjamin cut closest. He'd drop per-work metering for a public dividend, and my "you pay to keep it alive" has to survive that, since my line doesn't say who sets the price. Adam Becker is right that voluntary lab money is philanthropy wearing a costume. Leslie's "next DOI" warning lands on my procurement lever too: if a provost won't buy it, it doesn't count, but whose provost? Amy's opt-in training against Selena's free reuse is the same split I haven't squared: consent for training, openness for linking. Krakauer and Kara are my error-catchers question with data behind it. Later I want to push for one repeatable sentence, owners named, and funding from several sources.

Kenneth's synthesis got the centre right: pay for the checkers, not the tokens. What stuck with me was Nick's point that a lone researcher's price is zero. Fellowships without bargaining power still leave checkers as gig labour, and that's my consent argument coming back at me. Alex and Nick settled the audit question. It has to be independent, run on university servers, and not paid for by the labs. Jason's point that corrections donated into vendor databases amount to enclosure applies to my Wikipedia argument too. Sherry asked whether AI belongs in a given place at all, and I don't think "normal technology" answers her. Kara asked who will sign a contract. I want to name one I can push myself: open links back to sources, retraction checks, event-level audit rights, and a review date.
